Motor Insurance Portfolio: Profitability and Volatility

ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1

Jin Zhang

2026-05-01

This executive summary turns the technical analysis into a management-facing story. The objective is to identify where the motor insurance portfolio is profitable, where it is volatile, and which segments should be prioritised for underwriting or pricing review.

Contents

1BaselinePortfolio scale, premium, incurred loss and overall loss ratio.
2DistributionPremium shape, incurred loss skew and the policy-level loss tail.
3DriversPolicy type, coverage, claims history and payment frequency.
4ValidationDistribution tests and a claim frequency model with exposure offset.
5ActionsPractical underwriting and monitoring implications.

The deck moves from the whole portfolio into progressively sharper segment views. I first establish the baseline, then show the skewed distribution of losses, then move into policy type, coverage and customer signals. The final slides translate the evidence into actions.

Portfolio Baseline

Policy transactions354,140185,678 insured IDs across 2022-2024.
Exposure years250,325.9Exposure-weighted comparisons are used for frequency.
Total premiumEUR 105,079,669Portfolio scale before incurred loss.
Total incurredEUR 73,864,811Paid and reserved claim cost.
Loss ratio70.3%Profitable overall, but uneven by segment.
Underwriting profitEUR 31,214,859The headline hides a concentrated claims tail.

The portfolio contains 354,140 policy transactions and about 250,326 exposure years. The overall loss ratio is about 70.3%, which means the portfolio is profitable in aggregate. The important point is that aggregate profitability is not evenly distributed; we need segment and tail views to identify where underperformance and volatility are coming from.

Policy Mix

Combined cover is the largest premium block, followed by comprehensive-with-excess. Comprehensive-no-excess is smaller, but its colour already signals a weaker loss ratio. This tells us that a segment does not need to be the largest by premium to matter for portfolio quality.

Loss Distribution

88.1% of transactions have zero incurred loss, while 9.0% exceed break-even.

The portfolio is zero-inflated and right-skewed. Most transactions have no incurred loss, but the policies that do claim can produce a very wide range of costs. This is why mean loss ratio alone is not enough; volatility and tail concentration are central to the story.

2024 Deterioration

Loss ratio was stable around the mid-60% range in 2022 and 2023, then moved to about 74.7% in 2024. This does not necessarily mean one root cause; it tells us that year should be treated as an important context variable when interpreting the segment results.

Policy Type Drives Profitability

Comprehensive-no-excess has the highest loss ratio and the highest claim frequency. This makes intuitive business sense because no-excess policies expose the insurer to more small and medium claims. It is the clearest product-level candidate for pricing or deductible review.

Volatility Differs by Policy Type

Kruskal-Wallis and Fligner-Killeen tests both return p < 2.2e-16.

The difference is not just in average loss ratio. The distributions also differ in dispersion, which matters for volatility. Both tests strongly reject equality across policy types: the Kruskal-Wallis test validates distributional differences, while the Fligner-Killeen test validates variance differences.

Coverage View

Liability and property damage have the highest strategic importance because they combine large premium shares with high loss ratios. Occupants coverage has high average severity, but few claims, so it is more of a tail-monitoring issue than a broad profitability driver.

Customer Signals

Poor and neutral claims-history groups show weaker results than good claims-history policies. Semiannual and quarterly payment frequencies are also less favourable than annual payment. These variables may be proxies for customer mix or tenure, so they should be treated as diagnostic flags before being used directly as pricing actions.

Frequency Model

The model confirms that policy type remains the strongest signal after controlling for year, claims history, business origin, driver age, vehicle age, geography, payment frequency and fuel type. Comprehensive-no-excess is far above the third-party-only reference level, which supports the visual findings.

Tail Concentration

The top 1% of policy transactions by incurred loss accounts for about half of total incurred cost. This is the volatility story in one chart: underwriting and claims teams should not only track averages, but also build monitoring around large-loss concentration.

What To Do Next

1. DeductiblesReview comprehensive-no-excess pricing and deductible design.
2. 2024 DrilldownSeparate exposure growth from severity pressure in liability and property damage.
3. Tail WatchMonitor large-loss concentration instead of relying only on averages.
4. SelectionValidate payment and business-origin effects with tenure data.
5. Rating ReviewTest vehicle, fuel and circulation signals as candidate rating refinements.

The recommendations separate immediate portfolio review from longer-term modelling. The most direct action is the comprehensive-no-excess review. The second is to understand 2024 deterioration. The third is tail monitoring. The remaining actions should be explored with more data because they may represent customer selection effects rather than direct causes.

Limitations

Interpret as portfolio diagnostics, not final pricing indications. The dataset does not include exact geography, claim dates, inflation indices, driving usage, policy tenure, detailed no-claims discount history or external socioeconomic data.

The analysis is intentionally transparent and reproducible, but it is still constrained by the available variables. A production actuarial workflow would need exposure validation, claim development checks, external enrichment and out-of-sample testing before turning these insights into rating changes.
